verses.zh: 我看见主站在祭坛旁边；他说：你要击打柱顶，使门槛震动，打碎柱顶，落在众人头上；所剩下的人，我必用刀杀戮，无一人能逃避，无一人能逃脱。
verses.en: I saw the Lord[NOTE:1] standing by the altar[NOTE:2] and he said, “Strike the tops of the support pillars,[NOTE:3] so the thresholds shake!Knock them down on the heads of all the people,[NOTE:4] and I will kill the survivors[NOTE:5] with the sword.No one will be able to run away;[NOTE:6] no one will be able to escape.[NOTE:7]
notes: The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay).
The altar is perhaps the altar at Bethel.
Or “the capitals.” The Hebrew singular form is collective.

Heb “cut them off on the head of all of them.” The translation assumes the objective suffix on the verb refers to the tops of the pillars and that the following prepositional phrase refers to the people standing beneath. Another option is to take this phrase as referring to the pillars, in which case one could translate, “Knock all the tops of the pillars off.”

Heb “the remnant of them.” One could possibly translate, “every last one of them” (cf. NEB “to the last man”). This probably refers to those who survive the collapse of the temple, which may symbolize the northern kingdom.
Heb “a fugitive belonging to them will not run away.”
Heb “a survivor belonging to them will not escape.”

verses.zh: 他们虽然挖透阴间，我的手必取出他们来；虽然爬上天去，我必拿下他们来；
verses.en: Even if they could dig down into the netherworld,[NOTE:1] my hand would pull them up from there.Even if they could climb up to heaven,I would drag them down from there.
notes: Heb “into Sheol” (so ASV, NASB, NRSV), that is, the land of the dead localized in Hebrew thought in the earth’s core or the grave (cf. KJV “hell,” NCV, NLT “the place of the dead,” NIV84 “the depths of the grave,” NIV11 “the depths below”).

verses.zh: 虽然藏在迦密山顶，我必搜寻，捉出他们来；虽然从我眼前藏在海底，我必命蛇咬他们；
verses.en: Even if they were to hide on the top of Mount Carmel,I would hunt them down and take them from there.Even if they tried to hide from me[NOTE:1] at the bottom of the sea,from there[NOTE:2] I would command the Sea Serpent[NOTE:3] to bite them.
notes: Heb “from before my eyes.”
Or perhaps simply, “there,” if the מ (mem) prefixed to the adverb is dittographic (note the preceding word ends in mem).

If the article indicates a definite serpent, then the mythological Sea Serpent, symbolic of the world’s chaotic forces, is probably in view. See Job 26:13 and Isa 27:1 (where it is also called Leviathan). Elsewhere in the OT this serpent is depicted as opposing the Lord, but this text implies that even this powerful enemy of God is ultimately subject to his sovereign will.

verses.zh: 虽被仇敌掳去，我必命刀剑杀戮他们；我必向他们定住眼目，降祸不降福。
verses.en: Even when their enemies drive them into captivity,[NOTE:1] from there[NOTE:2] I will command the sword to kill them.I will not let them out of my sight;they will experience disaster, not prosperity.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Even if they go into captivity before their enemies.”
Or perhaps simply, “there,” if the מ (mem) prefixed to the adverb is dittographic (note the preceding word ends in mem).
Heb “I will set my eye on them for disaster, not good.”

verses.zh: 主―万军之耶和华摸地，地就消化，凡住在地上的都必悲哀。地必全然像尼罗河涨起，如同埃及河落下。
verses.en: The Sovereign Lord of Heaven’s Armies will do this.[NOTE:1] He touches the earth and it dissolves;[NOTE:2] all who live on it mourn.The whole earth[NOTE:3] rises like the Nile River[NOTE:4] and then grows calm[NOTE:5] like the Nile in Egypt.[NOTE:6]
notes: The words “will do this” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Or “melts.” The verb probably depicts earthquakes and landslides. See v. 5b.
Heb “all of it.”
Heb “the Nile.” The word “River” is supplied in the translation for clarity.
Or “sinks back down.”
See Amos 8:8, which is very similar to this verse.

verses.zh: 那在天上建造楼阁、在地上安定穹苍、命海水浇在地上的―耶和华是他的名。
verses.en: He builds the upper rooms of his palace[NOTE:1] in heavenand sets its foundation supports[NOTE:2] on the earth.[NOTE:3] He summons the water of the seaand pours it out on the earth’s surface.The Lord is his name.
notes: The MT reads “his steps.” If this is correct, then the reference may be to the steps leading up to the heavenly temple or the throne of God (cf. 1 Kgs 10:19-20). The prefixed מ (mem) may be dittographic (note the preceding word ends in mem). The translation assumes an emendation to עֲלִיָּתוֹ (ʿaliyyato, “his upper rooms”).

Traditionally, “vault” (so ASV, NAB, NRSV). The precise meaning of this word in this context is unclear. Elsewhere it refers to objects grouped or held together. F. I. Andersen and D. N. Freedman (Amos [AB], 845-46) suggest the foundational structure of a building is in view.
Verse 6a pictures the entire universe as a divine palace founded on the earth and extending into the heavens.

verses.zh: 耶和华说：以色列人哪，我岂不看你们如古实人吗？我岂不是领以色列人出埃及地，领非利士人出迦斐托，领亚兰人出吉珥吗？
verses.en: “You Israelites are just like the Ethiopians in my sight,”[NOTE:1] says the Lord. “Certainly I brought Israel up from the land of Egypt, but I also brought the Philistines from Caphtor[NOTE:2] and the Arameans from Kir.[NOTE:3]
notes: Though Israel was God’s special covenant people (see 3:2a), the Lord emphasizes they are not inherently superior to the other nations subject to his sovereign rule.tn The Hebrew text has a rhetorical question, “Are you children of Israel not like the Cushites to me?” The rhetorical question has been converted to an affirmative statement in the translation for clarity. See the comment at 8:8.
Caphtor may refer to the island of Crete.

The second half of v. 7 is also phrased as a rhetorical question in the Hebrew text, “Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor, and Aram from Kir?” The translation converts the rhetorical question into an affirmation for clarity.

verses.zh: 主耶和华的眼目察看这有罪的国，必将这国从地上灭绝，却不将雅各家灭绝净尽。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: Look, the Sovereign Lord is watching[NOTE:1] the sinful nation,[NOTE:2] and I will destroy it from the face of the earth.But I will not completely destroy the family[NOTE:3] of Jacob,” says the Lord.
notes: Heb “the eyes of the Sovereign Lord are on.”
Or “kingdom.”
Heb “house” (also in the following verse).

verses.zh: 我必出令，将以色列家分散在列国中，好像用筛子筛谷，连一粒也不落在地上。
verses.en: “For look, I am giving a command,and I will shake the family of Israel together with all the nations.It will resemble a sieve being shaken, when not even a pebble falls to the ground.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “like being shaken with a sieve, and a pebble does not fall to the ground.” The meaning of the Hebrew word צְרוֹר (tseror), translated “pebble,” is unclear here. In 2 Sam 17:13 it appears to refer to a stone. If it means “pebble,” then the sieve allows the grain to fall into a basket while retaining the debris and pebbles (cf. NIV). However, if one interprets צְרוֹר as a “kernel of grain” (cf. NASB, NKJV, NLT) then the sieve is constructed to retain the grain and allow the refuse and pebbles to fall to the ground. In either case, the simile supports the last statement in v. 8 by making it clear that God will distinguish between the righteous (the grain) and the wicked (the pebbles) when he judges, and will thereby preserve a remnant in Israel. Only the sinners will be destroyed (v. 10).

verses.zh: 我民中的一切罪人说：灾祸必追不上我们，也迎不着我们。他们必死在刀下。
verses.en: All the sinners among my people will die by the sword—the ones who say, ‘Disaster will not come near, it will not confront us.’

verses.zh: 到那日，我必建立大卫倒塌的帐幕，堵住其中的破口，把那破坏的建立起来，重新修造，像古时一样，
verses.en: “In that day I will rebuild the collapsing hut[NOTE:1] of David.I will seal its[NOTE:2] gaps,repair its[NOTE:3] ruins,and restore it to what it was like in days gone by.[NOTE:4]
notes: The phrase translated “collapsing hut” refers to a temporary shelter (cf. NASB, NRSV “booth”) in disrepair and emphasizes the relatively weakened condition of the once powerful Davidic dynasty. Others have suggested that the term refers to Jerusalem, while still others argue that it should be repointed to read “Sukkoth,” a garrison town in Transjordan. Its reconstruction would symbolize the rebirth of the Davidic empire and its return to power (e.g., M. E. Polley, Amos and the Davidic Empire, 71-74).

The MT reads a third feminine plural suffix, which could refer to the two kingdoms (Judah and Israel) or, more literally, to the breaches in the walls of the cities that are mentioned in v. 14 (cf. 4:3). Some emend to third feminine singular, since the “hut” of the preceding line (a feminine singular noun) might be the antecedent. In that case, the final nun (ן) is virtually dittographic with the vav (ו) that appears at the beginning of the following word.

The MT reads a third masculine singular suffix, which could refer back to David. However, it is possible that an original third feminine singular suffix (יה-, yod-he) has been misread as masculine (יו-, yod-vav). In later Hebrew script a ה (he) resembles a יו- (yod-vav) combination.
Heb “and I will rebuild as in days of antiquity.”

verses.zh: 使以色列人得以东所余剩的和所有称为我名下的国。此乃行这事的耶和华说的。
verses.en: As a result they[NOTE:1] will conquer those left in Edom[NOTE:2] and all the nations subject to my rule.”[NOTE:3] The Lord, who is about to do this, is speaking.
notes: They probably refers to the Israelites or to the Davidic rulers of the future.
Heb “take possession of the remnant of Edom”; cf. NASB, NIV, NRSV “possess the remnant of Edom.”

This verse envisions a new era of Israelite rule, perhaps patterned after David’s imperialistic successes (see 2 Sam 8-10). At the same time, however, the verse does not specify how this rule is to be accomplished. Note that the book ends with a description of peace and abundance, and its final reference to God (v. 15) does not include the epithet “the Lord who commands armies,” which has militaristic overtones. This is quite a different scene than what the book began with: nations at war and standing under the judgment of God.tn Heb “nations over whom my name is proclaimed.” The Hebrew idiom indicates ownership, sometimes as a result of conquest. See 2 Sam 12:28.

verses.zh: 耶和华说：日子将到，耕种的必接续收割的；踹葡萄的必接续撒种的；大山要滴下甜酒；小山都必流奶（原文是消化，见约珥三章十八节）。
verses.en: “Be sure of this,[NOTE:1] the time is[NOTE:2] coming,” says the Lord,“when the plowman will catch up to the reaper,[NOTE:3] and the one who stomps the grapes[NOTE:4] will overtake[NOTE:5] the planter.[NOTE:6] Juice will run down the slopes;[NOTE:7] it will flow down all the hillsides.[NOTE:8]
notes: Heb “behold” or “look.”
Heb “the days are.”

The plowman will catch up to the reaper. Plowing occurred in October-November, and harvesting in April-May (see P. King, Amos, Hosea, Micah, 109.) But in the future age of restored divine blessing, there will be so many crops the reapers will take all summer to harvest them, and it will be time for plowing again before the harvest is finished.

When the grapes had been harvested, they were placed in a press where workers would stomp on them with their feet and squeeze out the juice. For a discussion of grape-harvesting technique, see O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 110-12.
The verb is omitted here in the Hebrew text but has been supplied in the translation from the parallel line.

The grape harvest occurred in August-September, the planting in November-December (see P. King, Amos, Hosea, Micah, 109). But in the future age described here there will be so many grapes that the workers who stomp them will still be working when the next planting season arrives.
Or “hills,” where the vineyards were planted.
Heb “and all the hills will melt.”

verses.zh: 我必使我民以色列被掳的归回；他们必重修荒废的城邑居住，栽种葡萄园，喝其中所出的酒，修造果木园，吃其中的果子。
verses.en: I will bring back my people, Israel;[NOTE:1] they will rebuild the cities lying in rubble[NOTE:2] and settle down.[NOTE:3] They will plant vineyards and drink the wine they produce;[NOTE:4] they will grow orchards[NOTE:5] and eat the fruit they produce.[NOTE:6]
notes: This line can also be translated, “I will restore the fortunes of my people, Israel,” and is a common idiom (e.g., Deut 30:3; Jer 30:3; Hos 6:11; Zeph 3:20). This rendering is followed by several modern English versions (e.g., NEB, NRSV, NJPS).
Or “the ruined [or “desolate”] cities.”
Or “and live [in them].”
Heb “drink their wine.”
Or “gardens.”
Heb “eat their fruit.”

verses.zh: 我要将他们栽于本地，他们不再从我所赐给他们的地上拔出来。这是耶和华―你的　神说的。
verses.en: I will plant them on their land,and they will never again be uprooted from the[NOTE:1] land I have given them,”says the Lord your God.
notes: Heb “their.” The pronoun was replaced by the English definite article in the translation for stylistic reasons.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: AMOS 9:1-4

1I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, and He said,

"Smite the capitals so that the thresholds will shake,

And break them on the heads of them all!

Then I will slay the rest of them with the sword;

They will not have a fugitive who will flee,

Or a refugee who will escape.

2Though they dig into Sheol,

From there will My hand take them;

And though they ascend to heaven,

From there will I bring them down.

3Though they hide on the summit of Carmel,

I will search them out and take them from there;

And though they conceal themselves from My sight on the

floor of the sea,

From there I will command the serpent and it will bite them.

4And though they go into captivity before their enemies,

From there I will command the sword that it slay them,

And I will set My eyes against them for evil and not for good."

9:1 This refers to the destruction of a sacred worship site (i.e. altar, possibly at Bethel). The mechanism was the
earthquake (cf. Amos 1:1; 8:7-10; 9:1,9). The Israelites were trusting in their covenant relationship with YHWH,
but He rejected their amalgamated religious worship (cf. Amos 5:21-24; 8:10). Oh, the danger of eclectic worship!

▣ "Smite the capitals" The VERB (BDB 645, KB 697) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. This
verse has two IMPERATIVES and a Qal IMPERFECT used as a JUSSIVE
(i.e. "quake" BDB 950, KB 1271).

The term "capital" (BDB 499) refers to the carved (decorated) top of the support stone columns.

▣ "the thresholds" "Thresholds" (BDB 706) refers to the frame in which the door of the temple is mounted (cf. Isa. 6:4).

▣ "break them on the heads of them all" This is referring to the destruction of the worshipers by
supernatural means, similar to Samson destroying the Philistine temple in Jdg. 16:23-30. Here the mechanism seems
to have been a divinely timed and targeted earthquake.

▣ The last three lines of Amos 9:1 assert that no Israelite will ultimately escape YHWH's judgment
(cf. Amos 9:2-3, LXX, Peshitta, NRSV, REB, NET). It is similar in meaning to Amos 5:19.

Prophetic literature is characterized by judgment passages being placed beside salvation
passages. This chapter is a good example.

- Amos 9:1-10, judgment

- Amos 9:11-15, salvation

Both are true, but there are conditions/options based on YHWH's mercy and human faith/repentance. A
remnant of national Israel will survive to accomplish YHWH's redemptive plan (i.e. a Davidic King)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT (THREE SENSES)

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMTPIVE PLAN

9:2-3 These verses describe the futility of trying to escape from YHWH's judgment (e.g. Job 34:22; Jer. 23:24;
Isa. 29:15). The imagery used is the same as in Ps. 139:8, 9-12 (also note Prov. 15:11).

9:2 "Though they dig into Sheol" Sheol (BDB 982, e.g. Isa. 5:14; 14:9; 28:15,18; 38:10) refers to the
holding place of the dead. It is described as being in the earth (i.e. dig). This is similar to people trying to hide in
the caves in Isa. 2:10,19-21; Luke 23:30; and Rev. 6:15-16.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?, I. B.

▣ "My hand" ("My sight," v. 3) SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD

▣ "though they ascend to heaven" This is the spacial opposite of Sheol. The language of
these verses (i.e. Amos 9:1-4) is reminiscent of Ps. 139:8. There is no where to hide from an angry YHWH (cf. Heb. 10:31)!

In this verse heaven may refer to the atmosphere above the earth (cf. Gen. 1:1,14-19,20) and not
YHWH's throne (although Isa. 14:12-14 seems to merge the Jewish concept of the first heaven and the third heaven).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN

9:3 "the summit of Carmel" This may be dual imagery:

- this site had very thick vegetation (BDB 502 II) with many caves

- this was a traditional worship site (cf. 1 Kings 18)

▣ "though they conceal themselves from My sight on the floor of the sea" This is obviously
imagery for sinful mankind's attempt to hide from God (cf. Job 34:21-22; Ps. 139:9-12; Isa. 2:19-20; Jer. 16:16-17;
Hosea 10:8; Luke 23:30; Rev. 6:16).

The Israelites were a desert people. They were afraid of vast, deep water. The last place they would hide is the deep!

▣ "I will command the serpent and it will bite them" This is an allusion to the mythical sea monster,
Leviathan (cf. Job 3:8; 41:1; Ps. 74:13-14; 104:26; Isa. 27:1) or Rahab (cf. Job 9:13; 26:12; Ps. 89:10; Isa. 51:9). Notice
God commands (BDB 845, KB 1010, Piel IMPERFECT) the chaos monster.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SERPENT

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREAT RED DRAGON

9:4 This is a shocking verse. YHWH's anger and judgment will pursue them even into exile. They will be
herded like cattle into a foreign land, but even there death will await them! God will show no compassion
(cf. Hosea 1:6; 2:4) because they are no longer His covenant people (cf. Hosea 1:9; 2:23). This verse reflects the
consequences of breaking God's covenant (cf. Lev. 26, Deut. 28; esp. Amos 9:33).

▣ "I will set My eyes against them for evil and not for good" This is exactly opposite to the
covenant promises! This same imagery and terminology occur several times in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 21:10; 39:16;
44:11,27). It reflects the cursing and blessing sections of Leviticus 26 and especially Deuteronomy 27-29.

Notice that YHWH has the power to command actions outside of the Promised Land in the nations
supposedly controlled by other gods (LXX, Deut. 32:8). These other gods (i.e. elohim;
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.) are helpless. They are
non-existent and cannot stop YHWH's wrath!

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: AMOS 9:5-6

5The Lord God of hosts,

The One who touches the land so that it melts,

And all those who dwell in it mourn,

And all of it rises up like the Nile

And subsides like the Nile of Egypt;

6The One who builds His upper chambers in the heavens

And has founded His vaulted dome over the earth,

He who calls for the waters of the sea

And pours them out on the face of the earth,

The Lord is His name.

9:5-6 This is the last of the three doxologies, hymns, or poems to YHWH as creator (cf. Amos 4:13 and 5:8-9).

9:5 This may be another reference to "the earthquake," Amos 1:1; 8:8-9; 9:1 (i.e. the land, like the Nile River, rises and falls).

▣ "Lord God of hosts" This title is found in Amos 3:13; 4:13; 5:14,16,27;
6:8,14 (i.e. "God of hosts").

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (Adon and Kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

9:6 These are difficult-to-translate creation imagery. They speak of God as creator of heaven and earth
(i.e. Elohim, cf. Gen. 1; Ps. 104). He is the controller of heavenly bodies and water, both salt and fresh (i.e. forces of nature).

It is possible to translate "vaulted dome" (BDB 8) as "storehouse" and if so, then Amos 9:6a refers to YHWH's
dwelling place and Amos 9:6b refers to mankind's dwelling place, both of which are created by Him (cf. Amos 9:5a, 6d).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: AMOS 9:7-10

7"Are you not as the sons of Ethiopia to Me,

O sons of Israel?" declares the Lord.

"Have I not brought up Israel from the land of Egypt,

And the Philistines from Caphtor and the Arameans from Kir?

8Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are on the sinful kingdom,

And I will destroy it from the face of the earth;

Nevertheless, I will not totally destroy the house of Jacob,"

Declares the Lord.

9For behold, I am commanding,

And I will shake the house of Israel among all nations

As grain is shaken in a sieve,

But not a kernel will fall to the ground.

10All the sinners of My people will die by the sword,

Those who say, 'The calamity will not overtake or confront us.'

9:7-8 UBS, A Translator's Handbook on the Book of Amos, makes an interesting observation
on the relationship between Amos 9:7 and 8. Verse 7 states very emphatically that Israel is not special, unique,
or privileged, yet Amos 9:8 shows YHWH's special covenant care for her (cf. p. 181).

This same tension about God's covenant people exists in the New Testament.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "TENSIONS" (Excerpted from "Crucial Introductory Article" to the Book Revelation)

9:7 Both the questions of Amos 9:7 expect a "yes" answer. Basically YHWH is depreciating the
covenantal uniqueness of Israel. The one and only God (SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM)
has led all nations to and from their current geographical locations (cf. LXX, Deut. 32:8; and possibly implied in Deut. 29:26). It must have been
painful for Israel to be compared to Ethiopia, Philistia, and Syria. This is in sharp contrast to the election theology of Amos 3:2! Israel, like all
nations, will answer for their sins!

▣ "Israel from the land of Egypt" This is a reference to the Exodus, which was the beginning of Israel as a nation.

▣ "Caphtor" This refers to the island of Crete (BDB 499), which may have been the ancestral home of the
Philistines (sea people of the Aegean).

▣ "Kir" This (BDB 885 III) may refer to

- a part of Mesopotamia near Elam (cf. Isa. 21:2 and 22:6)

- a word which means "walls" (BDB 885 I, KB 1099) and stands for Nineveh (Kir means "city")

9:8 Israel will be treated like all other nations that sin, except that YHWH will not totally destroy
His people of promise (cf. Amos 5:4-7,14-15; 9:11-15). A righteous remnant of the house of Jacob will be
spared! This theme is often repeated in Jeremiah.

- Judah will survive, Jer. 4:27; 5:10,18; 33:16

- Israel will survive, Jer. 30:11; 31:35-36

God's eternal plan of redemption (i.e. the Messiah for all peoples) depends on it!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "the eyes of the Lord God are on the sinful nation" This idiom, "the
eyes of the Lord God," refers to His tender watchcare over His covenant people
(i.e. Deut. 11:12). However, the addition of the phrase, "the sinful nation," shows the dilemma. Maybe the best
way to express this is as a parent's pain at the poor life choices of a child (cf. Hosea 11). A truly loving parent
must let the consequences of poor choices play out for the long term health, happiness, and maturity of the child,
but it is very hurtful to both parties.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD

▣ "destroy" This term (BDB 1029, KB 1552) is used three times in this verse. It means "to annihilate,"
"to destroy," "to terminate." This is such a contrast to the use of this same term in Deut. 33:26-29, where it refers to YHWH destroying His
covenant people's enemies (i.e. Holy War).

Here, they are now the enemy (Hiphil PERFECT with waw). Yet even here there
is a glimmer of hope, "I will not totally destroy the house of Jacob" (Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
and a Hiphil IMPERFECT, a way to show intensity). Because of Amos 9:11 this could refer to Judah!

9:9-10 The Hebrew text is uncertain. Apparently this refers to some type of sifting process either for
judgment (i.e. pebble) or for salvation (i.e. grain kernels). The context implies the righteous remnant will be spared
and not one of them lost (i.e. Amos 9:9d). But for the wicked, YHWH will judge Israel like all other idolatrous nations
(i.e. Amos 9:10).

The VERB "shake" (BDB 631, KB 681, Hiphil PERFECT with waw
and Niphal PERFECT) refers to grain which is shaken through a sieve to remove the stones or dirt
clods that may be mixed in with the heads of grain.

The word translated "kernel" (NASB, NJB, while NKJ has "the smallest
grain") can also mean "pebble" (cf. 2 Sam. 17:13, KB 459; NRSV). This term (BDB 865) is usually translated "bundle," "parcel,"
"pouch," or "bag." Here it refers to an object caught in the bundling (reaping) process of stacking and tying grain stalks
together in the field.

"Among all nations" probably relates to Amos 9:4, where YHWH sends judgment even on those
sinful Israelites who are taken into exile. Even in other nations YHWH's judgment will destroy His faithless covenant
people (cf. Amos 9:10b). There is no place to hide from God's wrath (cf. Amos 5:19; Jer. 23:24; Ps. 139:7-12).

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: AMOS 9:11-12

11"In that day I will raise up the fallen booth of David,

And wall up its breaches;

I will also raise up its ruins

And rebuild it as in the days of old;

12That they may possess the remnant of Edom

And all the nations who are called by My name,"

Declares the Lord who does this.

9:11-15 The paragraph division is uncertain (all paragraph divisions are opinions, not inspiration; there is no textual marker
in Hebrew or Greek, except a repeated phrase or change of subject or speaker). The context shifts unexpectedly from judgment to restoration
(and from Samaria to Jerusalem). This shift of subjects is common in the Prophets. However, the message of hope is sure (i.e. Amos 5:14-15)!

9:11 "In that day" This phrase appears several times (cf. Amos 2:16; 8:3,9,18). See note at Amos 2:16. Israel
thought "that day" of YHWH's visitation would be a blessing, but Amos prophesied it would be a judgment
(e.g. Amos 5:18-20). Now Amos reverses the prophecy. For the righteous remnant "that day" will be a restoration of the
covenant promises to David (cf. 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17). In Amos 9:13-14 the promises of YHWH to Moses,
especially Deut. 28:1-14, are emphasized.

It is crucial we see that the prophets of the OT always look back to the Mosaic covenant stipulations. Moses
knew that the descendants of the Patriarchs could not keep the covenant (cf. Deut. 28:58-63; 29:25-28), as did Joshua
(cf. Josh. 24:19; see Paul's view in Galatians 3).

However, Deuteronomy also holds out hope that a future day of forgiveness and restoration provided by YHWH
will come (cf. Deut. 30:5) through His Messiah (cf. Deut. 18:18). It is this hope that the prophets pick up on and expand into an eschatological
day of victory and abundance, not judgment!

▣ "the fallen booth of David" This idiom refers to the kingdom of David, symbolized in Jerusalem as
its capital and spiritual center. The golden age of the United Monarchy (i.e. a godly king representing YHWH), with its
prosperity, security, and religious faithfulness is restored.

The prediction of a coming Messiah always goes back to Judah (cf. Genesis 49; 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17;
Isa. 7:14; 9:6-7; 11:1-9; Jer. 33:15,17; Micah 4:1-5; 5:2-5a).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA

▣ "its breaches" Verse 11 is literally a reference to the walls of Jerusalem. It is FEMININE
PLURAL (BDB 829), which may be a subtle way of referring to the reunification of Israel and Judah (i.e. one capital
and worship center).

9:12 This verse describes the military restoration to the limits of the Promised Land under David and
Solomon. This eschatological promise takes on universal implications in Acts 15:16-17, where "Edom" (MT) is changed
to "Adam" (i.e. mankind) in the Septuagint (see SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTAUGINT),
which is quoted by James (also note Paul's use of Hosea 1:10; 2:23 in Rom. 9:24-26)! This universal theme is also reflected in Amos 9:5-6,7
(cf. Gen. 3:15; 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6; Isa. 42:1,4,6,10-11; 49:6; 51:4; see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN).

This restoration to the Promised Land (e.g. Gen. 12:1-3; 13:14-17; 15:7) is in direct contrast to
Amos 9:1-4, 9-10. YHWH's relation to Abraham and his seed was based on covenant obedience. If they did not:

- they would "be destroyed," Deut. 4:26; 6:15; Josh. 23:15; 1 Kgs. 13:34; Amos 9:8

- they would be "plucked from" the land, Deut. 28:63

- they would be "uprooted," Deut. 29:28; 1 Kgs. 14:15; 2 Chr. 7:20

- they would "perish," Josh. 23:13,16

- they would be "cut off," 1 Kgs. 9:7

- they would "be carried away," 2 Kgs. 17:6,23; 18:9-11; 25:21 (also 23:27)

But if they obeyed, then they would remain in the land, 2 Kgs. 18:12; 21:8; 2 Chr. 33:8 (cf. 2 Sam. 7:10).

So often in the Prophets, YHWH's people returning to "their own land" is emphasized (cf. Isa. 14:1-2;
Jer. 16:15; Ezek. 11:17; 34:13,17; 36:24; 37:12,14,21; Amos 9:15).

13"Behold, days are coming," declares the Lord,

"When the plowman will overtake the reaper

And the treader of grapes him who sows seed;

When the mountains will drip sweet wine

And all the hills will be dissolved.

14Also I will restore the captivity of My people Israel,

And they will rebuild the ruined cities and live in them;

They will also plant vineyards and drink their wine,

And make gardens and eat their fruit.

15I will also plant them on their land,

And they will not again be rooted out from their land

Which I have given them,"

Says the Lord your God.

9:13-15 The time element of this verse must be eschatological, for the descendants of Abraham will be subjugated again
and again in history (i.e. Dan. 9:24-27). This promise (political peace and agricultural abundance, cf. Lev. 26:5, another
eschatological text is Joel 3:18) is still conditional on covenant obedience. This is not specifically stated, but surely implied.

9:13 "sweet wine" See SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

▣ "when the plowman will overtake the reaper" Amos is apparently restating Lev. 26:5. Obedience to the covenant brings prosperity.

9:14 This restoration is a reversal of Deut. 28:38-40; Amos 5:11; Micah 6:15; Zeph. 1:13. YHWH's people
will plant vineyards in His land and enjoy their fruit (i.e. imagery for security and longevity in the land,
e.g. Jer. 31:5; Ezek. 28:26; 1 Pet. 1:4-5).

9:15 Even this seemingly unconditional promise must be evaluated in light of the history of the Jewish
people. Obviously it has both an eschatological aspect (cf. 2 Sam. 7:10; Jer. 24:6; 32:41; 42:10) and a historical aspect.
